notes:
1. Meaning and Purpose of Directive Principles

  • Directive Principles of State Policy are constitutional instructions given to the State for establishing a just social, economic and political order.

They guide:

  • Parliament.
  • State Legislatures.
  • Union Executive.
  • State Executives.
  • Public authorities.
  • Governments while framing laws and policies.
  • They are contained in Part IV of the Constitution.
  • Part IV extends from Articles 36 to 51.
📌 Must-Memorise

DPSP → Part IV → Articles 36–51

2. Constitutional Objective of DPSP

  • Fundamental Rights primarily protect individual liberty and political democracy.

Directive Principles seek to establish:

  • Social democracy.
  • Economic democracy.
  • Welfare State.
  • Social justice.
  • Reduction of inequality.
  • Fair distribution of resources.
  • Dignified conditions of life.
  • Their central objective is to transform India from political democracy into a more comprehensive social and economic democracy.
📌 Must-Memorise

Fundamental Rights → Political Democracy

DPSP → Social + Economic Democracy

3. Welfare State

  • A Welfare State does more than maintain law and order.

It actively seeks to secure:

  • Education.
  • Health.
  • Employment.
  • Social security.
  • Fair wages.
  • Legal aid.
  • Nutrition.
  • Protection of vulnerable groups.
  • Balanced economic development.
  • Directive Principles provide the constitutional foundation for this welfare responsibility.
📌 Must-Memorise

DPSP → Constitutional Foundation of Welfare State

4. Instructions to the State

The State is expected to consider DPSPs while:

  • Enacting legislation.
  • Preparing budgets.
  • Creating welfare programmes.
  • Regulating labour.
  • Managing economic resources.
  • Developing rural institutions.
  • Protecting public health.
  • Protecting the environment.
  • DPSPs therefore influence both legislation and administration.

5. More than Political Promises

  • Directive Principles are not merely election promises or ordinary policy declarations.
  • They form part of the Constitution.
  • Governments are constitutionally expected to consider them in governance.
  • Their non-justiciability does not reduce them to political slogans.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

DPSP → Non-Justiciable

But Constitutionally Fundamental in Governance

6. Ambedkar's View

  • Dr. B.R. Ambedkar compared Directive Principles with the Instruments of Instructions under the Government of India Act, 1935.
  • Their constitutional purpose is to guide governments regarding the social and economic direction of the Republic.
📌 Must-Memorise

Ambedkar → DPSP Similar to Instruments of Instructions under 1935 Act

7. Political Accountability

  • Courts cannot ordinarily compel the State to implement a particular Directive Principle.

Governments remain accountable through:

  • Legislature.
  • Elections.
  • Public opinion.
  • Constitutional debate.
  • Audit.
  • Administrative review.
  • DPSPs therefore operate significantly through democratic and political responsibility.

8. Historical Development

Important stages include:

  • 1928 → Nehru Report.
  • 1931 → Karachi Resolution.
  • 1935 → Instruments of Instructions under Government of India Act.
  • 1937 → Constitution of Ireland.
  • 1950 → Part IV came into force.
📌 Must-Memorise

Immediate Constitutional Inspiration → Irish Constitution, 1937

9. Irish Constitutional Influence

  • The immediate constitutional inspiration for India's DPSP came from the Constitution of Ireland, 1937.
  • The Irish Constitution itself had been influenced by social-policy ideas in the Spanish constitutional tradition.
  • India adapted these ideas to its own social and economic conditions.
📌 Must-Memorise

DPSP → Ireland

Irish Model → Earlier Spanish Influence

10. Government of India Act, 1935

  • The Government of India Act, 1935 contained Instruments of Instructions.
  • These were directions issued to Governors and the Governor-General concerning exercise of certain powers.
  • Constitution-makers transformed this colonial administrative idea into democratic constitutional instructions directed to the State.

11. National Movement Influence

Directive Principles also reflect demands arising from:

  • Nehru Report, 1928.
  • Karachi Resolution, 1931.
  • Social-reform movements.
  • Labour movements.
  • Peasant demands.
  • Gandhian economic ideas.
  • Village-centred development.
  • Demand for social equality.
  • Opposition to colonial economic exploitation.

12. Karachi Resolution, 1931

The Karachi Resolution contained commitments relating to:

  • Civil liberties.
  • Labour protection.
  • Living wages.
  • Universal education.
  • State control of key industries.
  • Protection of women workers.
  • Economic justice.
  • It influenced both Fundamental Rights and Directive Principles.
📌 Must-Memorise

Karachi Resolution → 1931 → FR + DPSP Influence

13. Sapru Committee

The Sapru Committee distinguished constitutional rights into:

  • Justiciable rights.
  • Non-justiciable principles.

This distinction influenced the later separation between:

  • Part III — Fundamental Rights.
  • Part IV — Directive Principles.
📌 Must-Memorise

Sapru Committee → Justiciable Rights vs Non-Justiciable Principles

14. Why DPSP Were Made Non-Justiciable

The Constituent Assembly recognised that newly independent India faced:

  • Poverty.
  • Illiteracy.
  • Limited financial resources.
  • Weak public-health infrastructure.
  • Unequal land ownership.
  • Regional disparities.
  • Immediate judicial enforcement of every socio-economic promise was considered impractical.
  • DPSPs were therefore made non-justiciable but constitutionally fundamental in governance.

15. Instrument of Social Revolution

Directive Principles were designed as instruments of peaceful constitutional transformation.

They seek to replace:

  • Colonial economic structures.
  • Social hierarchy.
  • Extreme inequality.
  • Exploitative labour conditions.

with:

  • Welfare-oriented government.
  • Social justice.
  • Economic justice.
  • More equal social conditions.

16. Article 36 — Definition of State

  • Article 36 defines the expression “State” for Part IV.
  • Unless the context otherwise requires, it has the same meaning as in Part III.

It broadly includes:

  • Government and Parliament of India.
  • Government and Legislature of each State.
  • Local authorities.
  • Other authorities falling within the constitutional meaning of State.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 36 → State Defined Similar to Article 12

17. Article 12 vs Article 36

Article 12:

  • Defines State for Fundamental Rights.
  • Identifies authorities against whom rights may be enforced.

Article 36:

  • Uses substantially the same definition for DPSP.
  • Identifies authorities expected to apply Directive Principles in governance.

18. Article 37 — Nature of DPSP

Article 37 establishes two connected principles:

  • Directive Principles are not enforceable by any court.
  • They are fundamental in the governance of the country.
  • It is the duty of the State to apply them while making laws.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 37 → Non-Justiciable + Fundamental in Governance

19. Constitutional Balance under Article 37

  • DPSPs should not be treated as directly enforceable like Fundamental Rights.
  • They should also not be dismissed as legally meaningless political advice.
  • They are constitutional governance principles whose implementation depends substantially on legislation and public policy.

20. Progressive Implementation

The pace and method of implementation may depend upon:

  • Financial capacity.
  • Administrative feasibility.
  • Legislative choice.
  • Social conditions.
  • Competing constitutional demands.
  • The State nevertheless cannot treat Part IV as irrelevant.

21. Judicial Relevance of DPSP

Courts may use Directive Principles to:

  • Interpret Fundamental Rights.
  • Understand legislative purpose.
  • Assess reasonableness.
  • Expand social-justice principles.
  • Harmonise constitutional provisions.
  • Courts cannot ordinarily create an entire welfare programme solely from a Directive Principle.

22. Characteristics of DPSP

Directive Principles are:

  • Constitutional directions.
  • Non-justiciable.
  • Positive obligations on the State.
  • Welfare-oriented.
  • Dynamically applicable.
  • Broadly worded.
  • Politically enforceable through democratic accountability.
  • Important aids to constitutional interpretation.

23. Positive Obligations

Most Directive Principles require State action.

Examples include:

  • Provide legal aid.
  • Promote education.
  • Protect public health.
  • Organise Panchayats.
  • Reduce inequality.
  • Protect environment.
  • Promote social welfare.
📌 TNPSC Key Concept

DPSP → Mostly Positive Obligations on State

24. Broad Constitutional Language

DPSPs frequently use expressions such as:

  • Endeavour.
  • Promote.
  • Secure.
  • Direct its policy.
  • Take steps.
  • This language gives governments flexibility in choosing methods of implementation.

25. No Fixed Hierarchy among DPSPs

  • The Constitution does not declare one Directive Principle permanently superior to all others.

Governments may have to balance multiple principles according to:

  • Constitutional values.
  • Resources.
  • Social conditions.
  • Administrative priorities.

26. Classification of DPSP

For revision, DPSPs are commonly classified into:

  • Socialist Principles.
  • Gandhian Principles.
  • Liberal-Intellectual Principles.
  • This classification is scholarly.
  • The Constitution itself does not formally classify DPSPs in this manner.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Socialist/Gandhian/Liberal Classification → Academic

Not Constitutional Text

30. Article 38 — Social Order and Welfare

  • Article 38 directs the State to promote the welfare of the people.

The State should secure a social order in which:

  • Social justice.
  • Economic justice.
  • Political justice

inform all institutions of national life.

  • Article 38 forms a broad constitutional foundation for the Welfare State.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 38 → Social Order + Welfare

31. Article 38(2) — Reduction of Inequalities

  • Article 38(2) was inserted by the 44th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978.

It directs the State to minimise inequalities in:

  • Income.
  • Status.
  • Facilities.
  • Opportunities.

Inequalities should be reduced:

  • Among individuals.
  • Among different regions.
  • Among occupational groups.
📌 Must-Memorise

44th Amendment → Article 38(2)

32. Social, Economic and Political Justice under Article 38

Social Justice:

  • Reduces discrimination.
  • Opposes exploitation.
  • Promotes dignity and opportunity.

Economic Justice:

  • Promotes fair distribution of wealth.
  • Reduces poverty.
  • Supports employment and social security.

Political Justice:

  • Supports equal participation.
  • Equal voting rights.
  • Equal opportunity to hold public office.

33. Article 39 — Socio-Economic Justice

Article 39 directs State policy towards:

  • Adequate means of livelihood.
  • Equitable distribution of material resources.
  • Prevention of concentration of wealth.
  • Equal pay for equal work.
  • Protection of workers.
  • Protection of children.

34. Article 39(a) — Adequate Means of Livelihood

  • All citizens, men and women equally, should have the right to an adequate means of livelihood.
  • The objective is economic security and equal opportunity.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 39(a) → Adequate Livelihood

35. Article 39(b) — Material Resources

  • Ownership and control of material resources of the community should be distributed to best serve the common good.

Examples mentioned in the attached notes include:

  • Land.
  • Minerals.
  • Water resources.
  • Forests.
  • Energy resources.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 39(b) → Material Resources → Common Good

36. Article 39(c) — Concentration of Wealth

The economic system should not result in concentration of:

  • Wealth.
  • Means of production.
  • The principle seeks broader economic justice and prevention of monopoly-like concentration.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 39(c) → Prevent Concentration of Wealth

37. Article 39(d) — Equal Pay

  • Article 39(d) directs the State to secure equal pay for equal work for men and women.

It promotes:

  • Gender equality.
  • Fairness in employment.
  • Courts have treated it as an important constitutional principle in service jurisprudence.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 39(d) → Equal Pay for Equal Work

38. Article 39(e) — Worker Protection

  • Health and strength of workers should not be abused.

Citizens should not be compelled by economic necessity to enter occupations unsuited to:

  • Age.
  • Strength.
  • It promotes humane working conditions.

39. Article 39(f) — Protection of Children

Children should develop:

  • In a healthy manner.
  • In freedom.
  • With dignity.

They should be protected from:

  • Exploitation.

  • Material neglect.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 39(f) → Child Development + Protection

40. Article 39A — Equal Justice and Free Legal Aid

  • Article 39A was inserted by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976.

It directs the State to ensure:

  • Equal justice.
  • Equal opportunity before the legal system.
  • Free legal aid for eligible persons.
  • Economic or social disadvantage should not prevent access to justice.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 39A → Equal Justice + Free Legal Aid

42nd Amendment → Added

41. Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987

  • Parliament enacted the Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987 to implement Article 39A.

It provides:

  • Free legal services.
  • Legal awareness.
  • Alternative dispute resolution.
  • Lok Adalats.

42. NALSA and Legal Aid Structure

The legal-aid framework includes:

  • National Legal Services Authority — NALSA.
  • State Legal Services Authorities — SLSA.
  • District Legal Services Authorities — DLSA.
  • Taluk Legal Services Committees.

These institutions conduct:

  • Legal aid.
  • Legal literacy.
  • Lok Adalats.
  • Victim-compensation-related functions.

43. Lok Adalats

  • Lok Adalats are people's courts established under the Legal Services Authorities framework.

Their objectives include:

  • Speedy disposal.
  • Amicable settlement.
  • Low-cost justice.
  • Reduction of court burden.

Lok Adalat awards are:

  • Final.
  • Binding.
  • Treated as decrees of civil courts.
📌 Must-Memorise

Lok Adalat Award → Final + Binding + Deemed Civil Court Decree

44. Beneficiaries of Free Legal Aid

Eligible categories may include:

  • Scheduled Castes.
  • Scheduled Tribes.
  • Women.
  • Children.
  • Persons with disabilities.
  • Victims of trafficking.
  • Industrial workmen.
  • Persons in custody.
  • Economically weaker persons satisfying prescribed criteria.

45. Hussainara Khatoon v. State of Bihar, 1979

The Supreme Court held that:

  • Free legal aid is an essential element of fair procedure.
  • Speedy trial forms part of Article 21.
  • The case significantly strengthened access to justice.
📌 Must-Memorise

Hussainara Khatoon → 1979 → Free Legal Aid + Speedy Trial

46. Article 40 — Village Panchayats

  • Article 40 directs the State to organise Village Panchayats.
  • They should be endowed with powers necessary to function as units of local self-government.
  • The provision reflects Gandhi's idea of Gram Swaraj.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 40 → Village Panchayats

47. Gram Swaraj

Gandhian village-centred democracy emphasised:

  • Self-reliant villages.
  • Local solution of local problems.
  • Power flowing upward from people.
  • Grassroots participation.
  • Rural development.
  • Article 40 reflects this approach.

48. Article 40 and 73rd Amendment

  • Article 40 was originally only a Directive Principle.
  • The 73rd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1992 gave constitutional status to Panchayati Raj Institutions.

It inserted:

  • Part IX.
  • Articles 243–243O.
  • Eleventh Schedule.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 40 → Panchayats

73rd Amendment → Part IX + Eleventh Schedule

49. Article 41 — Work, Education and Public Assistance

Article 41 directs the State, within its economic capacity and development, to make effective provision for:

  • Right to work.
  • Right to education.
  • Public assistance.

Public assistance may be required in cases of:

  • Unemployment.
  • Old age.
  • Sickness.
  • Disability.
  • Other cases of undeserved want.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 41 → Work + Education + Public Assistance

50. Economic Capacity under Article 41

Article 41 expressly recognises limitations of:

  • Financial resources.
  • Economic development.
  • Administrative capacity.
  • Its objectives therefore require progressive implementation rather than immediate direct judicial enforcement.

51. Article 41 and Education

  • Before Article 21A was inserted, Article 41 helped support the constitutional objective of education.
  • After the 86th Amendment, education for ages 6–14 became a Fundamental Right under Article 21A.
  • Article 41 continues to support broader educational objectives beyond elementary education.

52. Article 42 — Humane Work Conditions and Maternity Relief

Article 42 directs the State to provide:

  • Just conditions of work.
  • Humane conditions of work.
  • Maternity relief.
  • It is closely connected with labour welfare and women's dignity.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 42 → Humane Work Conditions + Maternity Relief

53. Just and Humane Work Conditions

Such conditions may include:

  • Fair treatment.
  • Reasonable working hours.
  • Weekly rest.
  • Workplace safety.
  • Sanitation.
  • Drinking water.
  • Rest intervals.
  • Medical and welfare facilities.
  • Protection against exploitation.

54. Maternity Relief

Maternity relief protects women during:

  • Pregnancy.
  • Childbirth.
  • Postnatal recovery.
  • Early childcare.

It supports:

  • Health.
  • Employment security.
  • Economic independence.
  • Dignity.
  • Equal participation in employment.

Article 42 complements:

  • Article 14 → Equality.

  • Article 21 → Life and dignity.

56. Article 43 — Living Wage

Article 43 directs the State to endeavour to secure for workers:

  • Work.
  • Living wage.
  • Decent standard of life.
  • Leisure.
  • Social opportunities.
  • Cultural opportunities.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 43 → Living Wage + Decent Standard of Life

57. Minimum Wage, Fair Wage and Living Wage

Minimum Wage:

  • Basic legally acceptable wage.
  • Intended to meet subsistence needs.

Fair Wage:

  • Higher than minimum wage.
  • Influenced by industry capacity, productivity and prevailing wage levels.

Living Wage:

  • Broader constitutional ideal.
  • Supports food, clothing, housing, healthcare, education, social security, recreation and cultural participation.
⚠️ TNPSC Favourite

Article 43 Specifically Mentions → Living Wage

58. Leisure under Article 43

  • Article 43 treats leisure as part of worker welfare.

It supports protections relating to:

  • Reasonable working hours.
  • Weekly holidays.
  • Paid leave.
  • Rest periods.
  • Leisure is treated as part of a dignified life.

59. Cottage Industries

  • Article 43 also directs the State to promote cottage industries.

They may be organised:

  • Individually.
  • Cooperatively.
  • Particularly in rural areas.
  • The provision reflects Gandhian economic thinking.

60. Importance of Cottage Industries

Cottage industries may support:

  • Rural employment.
  • Local skills.
  • Traditional crafts.
  • Women's participation.
  • Decentralised production.
  • Reduction of migration.
  • Village self-reliance.

61. Article 43A — Workers' Participation in Management

  • Article 43A was inserted by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976.

It directs the State to secure participation of workers in management of:

  • Industries.
  • Establishments.
  • Other organisations engaged in production.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 43A → Workers in Management

42nd Amendment → Added

62. Industrial Democracy

  • Article 43A supports the idea of industrial democracy.
  • Workers should have a meaningful voice in matters affecting them.

Participation may occur through:

  • Works committees.
  • Joint management councils.
  • Worker representatives.
  • Consultative committees.
  • Board-level representation where provided.
  • Collective bargaining mechanisms.

63. Worker Participation Does Not Mean Ownership

Participation in management does not automatically mean:

  • Worker ownership.
  • Complete worker control over business decisions.
  • It generally refers to consultative or representative involvement under law.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Article 43A → Worker Participation

Not Automatic Worker Ownership

  • Livestock nutrition.
  • Humane management.

89. Cattle Preservation

Article 48 directs the State to take steps for prohibiting slaughter of:

  • Cows.
  • Calves.
  • Other milch cattle.
  • Draught cattle.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 48 → Cows + Calves + Milch + Draught Cattle

90. Article 48 Is Not Directly Penal

  • Article 48 itself does not create a directly enforceable criminal offence.
  • States enact laws within their legislative competence.
  • Such laws remain subject to constitutional review.

91. Article 48A — Environment

Article 48A directs the State to:

  • Protect the environment.
  • Improve the environment.
  • Safeguard forests.
  • Safeguard wildlife.
  • It was inserted by the 42nd Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 48A → Environment + Forests + Wildlife

42nd Amendment → Added

92. Shared Environmental Responsibility

  • Article 48A → Duty of State.
  • Article 51A(g) → Duty of citizens.
  • Article 21 → Judicially expanded protection of life and healthy environment.
📌 Must-Memorise

48A → State

51A(g) → Citizen

21 → Judicial Environmental Protection

93. Environmental Principles

Courts have used principles such as:

  • Sustainable development.
  • Precautionary principle.
  • Polluter pays principle.
  • Public trust doctrine.
  • Intergenerational equity.

94. Important Environmental Cases

  • Rural Litigation and Entitlement Kendra v. State of Uttar Pradesh → Ecological damage from limestone quarrying.
  • M.C. Mehta cases → Environmental protection under Article 21 with Articles 48A and 51A(g).
  • Vellore Citizens' Welfare Forum v. Union of India, 1996 → Sustainable development, precautionary principle and polluter pays principle.
📌 Must-Memorise

Vellore Citizens → 1996 → Sustainable Development + Precaution + Polluter Pays

95. Article 49 — Monuments

Article 49 places a duty on the State to protect monuments, places and objects declared by or under parliamentary law to be of:

  • National importance.
  • Artistic importance.
  • Historic importance.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 49 → Monuments of National Importance

96. Heritage Protected under Article 49

Protected heritage may include:

  • Archaeological sites.
  • Ancient monuments.
  • Historic structures.
  • Sculptures.
  • Inscriptions.
  • Objects of artistic value.
  • Nationally important cultural remains.

97. State Responsibility under Article 49

The State must protect such heritage against:

  • Destruction.
  • Removal.
  • Disposal.
  • Export.
  • Damage.
  • Alteration.
  • Disfigurement.

98. Article 49 and Article 51A(f)

  • Article 49 places a duty on the State to protect nationally important heritage.
  • Article 51A(f) places a duty on citizens to value and preserve India's composite culture.
📌 Must-Memorise

Heritage → State: Article 49

Citizen: Article 51A(f)

99. Article 50 — Separation of Judiciary from Executive

Article 50 directs the State to separate:

  • Judiciary.
  • Executive

in public services of the State.

  • It particularly concerns subordinate judicial independence.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 50 → Separation of Judiciary from Executive

100. Purpose of Article 50

Separation promotes:

  • Judicial independence.
  • Fair trial.
  • Impartial adjudication.
  • Rule of Law.
  • Protection from executive pressure.

101. Judicial and Executive Magistrates

Separation between:

  • Judicial Magistrates.
  • Executive Magistrates

reflects the objective of Article 50.

  • India follows functional separation rather than absolute separation of powers.

102. Article 51 — International Peace and Security

Article 51 directs the State to endeavour to:

  • Promote international peace and security.
  • Maintain just and honourable relations between nations.
  • Foster respect for international law and treaty obligations.
  • Encourage settlement of international disputes by arbitration.
📌 Must-Memorise

Article 51 → International Peace + International Law + Arbitration

103. Article 51 Clause Mapping

  • Article 51(a) → International peace and security.
  • Article 51(b) → Just and honourable relations.
  • Article 51(c) → Respect for international law and treaty obligations.
  • Article 51(d) → Arbitration of international disputes.

104. International Law in India

  • International treaties do not automatically become directly enforceable domestic law in every case merely through signature or ratification.
  • Where domestic legal change is required, Parliament may enact legislation.

Courts may refer to international conventions where:

  • Domestic law is silent.
  • Convention is not inconsistent with legislation.
  • Constitutional rights support such interpretation.

105. Implementation of DPSP

Directive Principles are implemented through:

  • Constitutional amendments.
  • Parliamentary legislation.
  • State legislation.
  • Government policies.
  • Welfare programmes.
  • Judicial interpretation.
  • Local-government institutions.

106. Land Reform

Land-reform measures sought to implement Articles 38 and 39 through:

  • Zamindari abolition.
  • Removal of intermediaries.
  • Land ceilings.
  • Tenancy reform.
  • Redistribution of agricultural land.
  • Ninth Schedule protections were initially used in connection with several land-reform laws.

107. Labour Welfare

Articles 39, 41, 42, 43 and 43A have influenced laws and policies concerning:

  • Minimum wages.
  • Equal remuneration.
  • Maternity relief.
  • Workplace safety.
  • Social security.
  • Trade unions.
  • Worker participation.
  • Employment injury compensation.

108. Legal Aid Implementation

Article 39A has been implemented through:

  • Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987.
  • NALSA.
  • State and District Legal Services Authorities.
  • Lok Adalats.
  • Free legal services.
  • Legal-literacy programmes.

109. Education Implementation

The constitutional education framework includes:

  • Article 21A.
  • Revised Article 45.
  • Right of Children to Free and Compulsory Education Act, 2009.
  • Early childhood-care programmes.

110. Social Security and Public Health

Articles 41 and 47 support measures relating to:

  • Old-age assistance.
  • Disability support.
  • Unemployment relief.
  • Food security.
  • Public health.
  • Maternal welfare.
  • Child nutrition.

111. Protection of Weaker Sections

Article 46 supports:

  • Reservations.
  • Scholarships.
  • Hostels.
  • Educational support.
  • Scheduled Area protections.
  • Economic-development programmes.
  • Laws against exploitation and atrocities.

112. Cottage and Cooperative Sectors

Articles 43 and 43B support:

  • Village industries.
  • Handloom and handicrafts.
  • Dairy cooperatives.
  • Agricultural credit societies.
  • Marketing cooperatives.
  • Rural self-employment.

113. Constitutional Limitation on DPSP Implementation

  • A law does not become constitutionally valid merely because it claims to implement a Directive Principle.

It must still comply with:

  • Fundamental Rights.
  • Legislative competence.
  • Basic Structure.
  • Other constitutional limitations.
📌 TNPSC Key Concept

DPSP Objective ≠ Automatic Validity of Every Law

114. Champakam Dorairajan, 1951

  • In State of Madras v. Champakam Dorairajan, the Supreme Court held that a Directive Principle could not override an enforceable Fundamental Right.

The decision led to:

  • First Constitutional Amendment Act, 1951.
  • Article 15(4).
📌 Must-Memorise

Champakam Dorairajan → 1951 → FR Prevailed in Direct Conflict

115. In Re Kerala Education Bill, 1958

The Supreme Court encouraged harmonious interpretation between:

  • Fundamental Rights.
  • Directive Principles.
  • It helped move constitutional interpretation away from rigid conflict.

116. Golak Nath v. State of Punjab, 1967

  • The Supreme Court held that Parliament could not amend Fundamental Rights.
  • This position was later changed through constitutional amendments and overruled in Kesavananda Bharati.
📌 Must-Memorise

Golak Nath → 1967 → Earlier Restriction on FR Amendment

117. Twenty-Fourth Amendment

The 24th Constitutional Amendment affirmed Parliament's power to amend:

  • Any part of the Constitution.
  • Including Fundamental Rights.

118. Article 31C

  • Article 31C was inserted by the 25th Constitutional Amendment Act, 1971.

It originally protected laws intended to implement:

  • Article 39(b).
  • Article 39(c)

from challenge under specified Fundamental Rights.

📌 Must-Memorise

25th Amendment → Article 31C

31C → Article 39(b) + 39(c)

119. Kesavananda Bharati, 1973

  • Parliament may amend Fundamental Rights.
  • Parliament cannot destroy the Basic Structure.
  • Part III and Part IV must be understood as part of the complete constitutional scheme.
📌 Must-Memorise

Kesavananda Bharati → 1973 → Basic Structure

120. Forty-Second Amendment and Article 31C

  • The 42nd Amendment attempted to extend Article 31C protection to laws implementing all Directive Principles.
  • This attempted to give much broader primacy to Part IV.

121. Minerva Mills, 1980

  • The Supreme Court struck down the 42nd Amendment's extension of Article 31C to all DPSPs.

It held that:

  • Harmony between Fundamental Rights and DPSP forms part of the Basic Structure.
  • Absolute primacy of all DPSPs over Fundamental Rights would damage the Constitution.
📌 Must-Memorise

Minerva Mills → 1980 → Harmony between Part III and Part IV

122. Present FR-DPSP Relationship

The accepted constitutional principle is:

  • Fundamental Rights and DPSPs are complementary.
  • Neither is permanently superior in every situation.
  • Courts seek harmonious interpretation.
  • Article 31C protection remains principally connected with Article 39(b) and 39(c), subject to constitutional doctrine and judicial interpretation.

123. DPSP and Fundamental Duties

Directive Principles:

  • Addressed to State.
  • Part IV.
  • Articles 36–51.

Fundamental Duties:

  • Addressed to citizens.
  • Part IVA.
  • Article 51A.
  • Both contribute to constitutional transformation but operate upon different actors.

124. Environment Link

  • Article 48A → State environmental duty.
  • Article 51A(g) → Citizen environmental duty.
  • Article 21 → Judicially expanded environmental right dimension.

125. Education Link

  • Article 45 → Early childhood care by State.
  • Article 21A → Free and compulsory education for ages 6–14.
  • Article 51A(k) → Parent or guardian educational responsibility.

126. Heritage Link

  • Article 49 → State duty to protect nationally important monuments.
  • Article 51A(f) → Citizen duty to preserve composite culture.

127. First Constitutional Amendment Act, 1951

  • Inserted Article 15(4).
  • Added the Ninth Schedule.
  • Supported social-reform and land-reform objectives after Champakam Dorairajan.
📌 Must-Memorise

1st Amendment → Article 15(4) + Ninth Schedule

128. Fourth Constitutional Amendment Act, 1955

Expanded constitutional support for:

  • Land-reform measures.
  • State acquisition of property.
  • Socio-economic legislation.

129. Seventeenth Constitutional Amendment Act, 1964

  • Added further agrarian-reform laws to the Ninth Schedule.
  • It strengthened protections connected with land reform.

130. Twenty-Fifth Constitutional Amendment Act, 1971

  • Inserted Article 31C.
  • Its principal purpose was to protect laws implementing Article 39(b) and 39(c) from challenge under specified rights.

131. Forty-Second Constitutional Amendment Act, 1976

Important DPSP-related changes:

  • Article 39A → Equal justice and free legal aid.
  • Article 43A → Workers' participation in management.
  • Article 48A → Environmental protection.
  • Attempted extension of Article 31C to all DPSPs.
📌 Ultra-Short Memory

42nd → Legal Aid + Worker Participation + Environment

132. Forty-Fourth Constitutional Amendment Act, 1978

  • Inserted Article 38(2).

Directed the State to minimise inequalities in:

  • Income.
  • Status.
  • Facilities.
  • Opportunities.
  • It also removed Right to Property from Part III and preserved property protection under Article 300A.

133. Eighty-Sixth Constitutional Amendment Act, 2002

It:

  • Inserted Article 21A.
  • Substituted Article 45.
  • Added Article 51A(k).
📌 Must-Memorise

86th Amendment → Education Framework

134. Ninety-Seventh Constitutional Amendment Act, 2011

  • Inserted Article 43B.

Promoted:

  • Voluntary cooperative formation.
  • Autonomy.
  • Democratic control.
  • Professional management.

135. Waman Rao v. Union of India, 1981

  • The case dealt with Ninth Schedule review.
  • Post-Kesavananda constitutional developments remain subject to Basic Structure scrutiny.

136. Randhir Singh v. Union of India, 1982

The Supreme Court connected equal pay for equal work with:

  • Article 14.
  • Article 16.
  • Article 39(d).
📌 Must-Memorise

Randhir Singh → 1982 → Equal Pay for Equal Work

137. Olga Tellis v. Bombay Municipal Corporation, 1985

  • The Supreme Court recognised the right to livelihood within Article 21 reasoning.
  • The decision reflected socio-economic constitutional principles.

138. Unni Krishnan v. State of Andhra Pradesh, 1993

  • The case dealt with education.
  • It contributed to the constitutional evolution that later resulted in Article 21A.

139. Mirzapur Moti Kureshi Case, 2005

  • The Supreme Court examined cattle-preservation legislation.
  • Article 48 was considered along with Fundamental Rights and contemporary social conditions.

140. Rajendra N. Shah Case, 2021

  • The Supreme Court examined the 97th Amendment provisions concerning cooperative societies.
  • State ratification was required for certain provisions affecting State cooperatives.
  • Article 43B remained valid.
📌 Must-Memorise

Rajendra N. Shah → 2021 → Cooperative Amendment + State Ratification

Article 43B → Remained Valid

141. Important Article Mapping

  • Article 36 → Definition of State.
  • Article 37 → Nature of DPSP.
  • Article 38 → Social order and welfare.
  • Article 39 → Socio-economic justice.
  • Article 39A → Equal justice and legal aid.
  • Article 40 → Village Panchayats.
  • Article 41 → Work, education and public assistance.
  • Article 42 → Humane work conditions and maternity relief.
  • Article 43 → Living wage and cottage industries.
  • Article 43A → Workers' participation.
  • Article 43B → Cooperative societies.
  • Article 44 → Uniform Civil Code.
  • Article 45 → Early childhood care and education.
  • Article 46 → Weaker sections.
  • Article 47 → Nutrition and public health.
  • Article 48 → Agriculture and animal husbandry.
  • Article 48A → Environment.
  • Article 49 → Monuments.
  • Article 50 → Judiciary–Executive separation.
  • Article 51 → International peace.

142. Amendment Mapping

  • 1st Amendment, 1951 → Article 15(4) + Ninth Schedule.
  • 4th Amendment, 1955 → Property and socio-economic reform support.
  • 17th Amendment, 1964 → Further agrarian laws in Ninth Schedule.
  • 25th Amendment, 1971 → Article 31C.
  • 42nd Amendment, 1976 → Articles 39A, 43A and 48A.
  • 44th Amendment, 1978 → Article 38(2).
  • 86th Amendment, 2002 → Article 21A + revised Article 45 + Article 51A(k).
  • 97th Amendment, 2011 → Article 43B.

143. Case Mapping

  • Champakam Dorairajan, 1951 → FR vs DPSP.
  • In Re Kerala Education Bill, 1958 → Harmonious interpretation.
  • Golak Nath, 1967 → Earlier restriction on amendment of FR.
  • Kesavananda Bharati, 1973 → Basic Structure.
  • Hussainara Khatoon, 1979 → Legal aid + speedy trial.
  • Minerva Mills, 1980 → FR-DPSP harmony.
  • Waman Rao, 1981 → Ninth Schedule review.
  • Randhir Singh, 1982 → Equal pay.
  • Shah Bano, 1985 → Article 44.
  • Olga Tellis, 1985 → Livelihood.
  • Unni Krishnan, 1993 → Education.
  • Sarla Mudgal, 1995 → Article 44.
  • Vellore Citizens, 1996 → Environmental principles.
  • John Vallamattom, 2003 → Article 44.
  • Mirzapur Moti Kureshi, 2005 → Article 48.
  • Rajendra N. Shah, 2021 → Cooperatives.

144. TNPSC Traps

  • DPSP → Part IV.
  • Part IV → Articles 36–51.
  • Immediate source → Irish Constitution.
  • DPSP → Non-justiciable.
  • Article 37 → Fundamental in governance.
  • Article 36 → Same broad State definition as Article 12.
  • DPSP classification → Scholarly, not constitutional.
  • Article 38 → Welfare and social order.
  • Article 38(2) → 44th Amendment.
  • Article 39(a) → Livelihood.
  • Article 39(b) → Material resources.
  • Article 39(c) → Concentration of wealth.
  • Article 39(d) → Equal pay.
  • Article 39(e) → Workers' health.
  • Article 39(f) → Children.
  • Article 39A → Legal aid.
  • Article 39A → 42nd Amendment.
  • Article 40 → Village Panchayats.
  • Article 41 → Work + education + public assistance.
  • Article 42 → Humane work + maternity relief.
  • Article 43 → Living wage + cottage industries.
  • Article 43A → Workers' participation.
  • Article 43B → Cooperatives.
  • Article 44 → UCC.
  • Article 45 → Below six years.
  • Article 46 → Weaker sections + SC/ST.
  • Article 47 → Nutrition + public health + intoxicants.
  • Article 48 → Agriculture + animal husbandry + cattle preservation.
  • Article 48A → Environment.
  • Article 49 → Monuments.
  • Article 50 → Judiciary–Executive separation.
  • Article 51 → International peace.
  • 73rd Amendment → Panchayats.
  • 86th Amendment → 21A + Article 45 + 51A(k).
  • 97th Amendment → Article 43B.
  • Champakam Dorairajan → FR prevailed in direct conflict.
  • Article 31C → Article 39(b) and 39(c).
  • Minerva Mills → FR-DPSP harmony.
  • Below 6 → Article 45.
  • Ages 6–14 → Article 21A.
  • Parent duty → Article 51A(k).
  • Environment State duty → 48A.
  • Environment citizen duty → 51A(g).
  • Article 44 → Not directly enforceable.
  • Article 48 → Does not itself create a criminal offence.
  • Article 47 → Does not itself impose nationwide prohibition.
  • DPSP objective alone → Cannot validate an unconstitutional law.

Ultra-Short Memory Chain

  • Part IV → 36–51.
  • 36 → State.
  • 37 → Non-Justiciable.
  • 38 → Welfare.
  • 39 → Socio-Economic Justice.
  • 39A → Legal Aid.
  • 40 → Panchayats.
  • 41 → Work/Education/Assistance.
  • 42 → Work + Maternity.
  • 43 → Living Wage.
  • 43A → Workers.
  • 43B → Cooperatives.
  • 44 → UCC.
  • 45 → Below 6.
  • 46 → Weaker Sections.
  • 47 → Nutrition + Health.
  • 48 → Agriculture + Cattle.
  • 48A → Environment.
  • 49 → Monuments.
  • 50 → Judiciary–Executive.
  • 51 → International Peace.
  • Ireland → DPSP.
  • 42nd → 39A + 43A + 48A.
  • 44th → 38(2).

  • Golak Nath → 1967.
  • Kesavananda → 1973.
  • Minerva Mills → 1980.
